en: Thus have I heard— Majjhima Nikāya 26, the Discourse on the Pile of Bones (Pāsarāsi Sutta).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Meanwhile, a number of bhikkhus approached the Venerable Ānanda and said to him:
“It has been a long time, friend Ānanda, since we have heard a Dhamma talk from the Blessed One’s own presence.
It would be good, friend Ānanda, if we could hear a Dhamma talk from the Blessed One’s own presence.
“In that case, venerable sirs, go to the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka.”
“Perhaps you might obtain the opportunity to hear a discourse on the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One.
“Very well, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ānanda.
Then, having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from his almsround after the meal, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Come, Ānanda, let us go to the Eastern Park, to Migāra’s Mother’s Mansion, for the day’s rest.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, together with the Venerable Ānanda, went to the Eastern Park, to Migāra’s Mother’s Mansion, for the day’s rest.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Come, Ānanda, let us go to the Eastern Bathing Place to bathe our limbs.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One went with the Venerable Ānanda to the Eastern Bathing Place to bathe his limbs.
Having bathed his limbs at the Eastern Bathing Place and having stepped out, he stood there wearing a single robe, drying his limbs.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka is not far from here.
Venerable sir, the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka is delightful;
venerable sir, the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka is inspiring.”
“It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would go to the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka out of compassion.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then the Blessed One went to the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka.
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus were seated together in the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka, engaged in a discussion on the Dhamma.
Then the Blessed One stood outside the gateway, waiting for the conclusion of their conversation.
When the Blessed One perceived that the conversation had ended, he coughed and knocked on the door.
Those monks opened the door for the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having entered the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka, sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks, for what discussion have you gathered here now? And what was the conversation of yours that remained unfinished?
“Venerable sir, it was a discussion concerning the Dhamma, centered on the Blessed One himself, which remained unfinished when the Blessed One arrived.
“Good, monks.”
This, monks, is what is fitting for you, sons of good family who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith: that you should sit together in discourse on the Dhamma.
When you have gathered together, monks, two things are to be practiced:
either discourse on the Dhamma or noble silence.
"Bhikkhus, there are these two kinds of search:
the noble search and the ignoble search. And what, bhikkhus, is the ignoble search?"
In this case, monks, a certain person, being himself subject to birth, seeks after that which is subject to birth;
being himself subject to aging, he seeks after that which is subject to aging; being himself subject to illness, he seeks after that which is subject to illness;
being himself subject to death, he seeks after that which is subject to death; being himself subject to sorrow...
Being subject to sorrow, one seeks only that which is subject to sorrow; being subject to defilement oneself, one seeks only that which is subject to defilement.
And what, monks, do you say is subject to birth?

Wife and children, monks, are subject to birth; male and female slaves are subject to birth; goats and sheep are subject to birth; chickens and pigs are subject to birth; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to birth; gold and silver are subject to birth.
"Bhikkhus, these acquisitions are subject to birth.
Herein, being bound, infatuated, and obsessed by them, one who is himself subject to birth seeks only that which is subject to birth.
And what, bhikkhus, do you say is subject to aging?"

“Monks, sons and wives are subject to aging; male and female slaves are subject to aging; goats and sheep are subject to aging; chickens and pigs are subject to aging; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to aging;
gold and silver are subject to aging. These acquisitions, monks, are subject to aging.
Bound, infatuated, and obsessed with these, one who is himself subject to aging seeks only that which is subject to aging.”
And what, monks, do you say is subject to sickness?

Wife and children, monks, are subject to sickness; male and female slaves are subject to sickness; goats and sheep are subject to sickness; chickens and pigs are subject to sickness; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to sickness.
These acquisitions, monks, are subject to sickness.
"Herein, being attached, infatuated, and clinging, though himself subject to illness, he seeks out what is subject to illness.
And what, monks, do you say is subject to death?

Wife and children, monks, are subject to death; male and female slaves are subject to death; goats and sheep are subject to death; chickens and pigs are subject to death; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to death."
"Bhikkhus, these acquisitions (upadhī) are subject to death.
Herein, being attached, infatuated, and clinging to them, one who is himself subject to death seeks only that which is subject to death.
And what, bhikkhus, do you call 'subject to sorrow'?"

“Monks, wife and children are subject to sorrow; male and female slaves are subject to sorrow; goats and sheep are subject to sorrow; chickens and pigs are subject to sorrow; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to sorrow.
These acquisitions, monks, are subject to sorrow.
Bound, infatuated, and obsessed with these, being himself subject to sorrow, he seeks only that which is subject to sorrow.”
And what, monks, do you say is subject to defilement?
Wife and children, monks, are subject to defilement; male and female slaves are subject to defilement; goats and sheep are subject to defilement;
chickens and pigs are subject to defilement; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to defilement.
Gold and silver are subject to defilement.
These acquisitions, monks, are indeed subject to defilement.
Herein, one who is tied, infatuated, and obsessed with them—being himself subject to defilement—seeks only that which is subject to defilement.
This, monks, is the ignoble quest.
And what, monks, is the noble quest?
Here, monks, someone being himself subject to birth, having understood the danger in being subject to birth, seeks the unborn—

He seeks Nibbāna, the unsurpassed security from bondage; being himself subject to aging, having understood the danger in that which is subject to aging, he seeks Nibbāna, the ageless, the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Being himself subject to illness, having understood the danger in that which is subject to illness, he seeks Nibbāna, the unailing, the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Being himself subject to death, having understood the danger in that which is subject to death, he seeks the Deathless, the unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna;

being himself subject to sorrow, having understood the danger in that which is subject to sorrow, he seeks the sorrowless, the unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna; being himself subject to defilement... [in that which is subject to defilement].
Having understood the danger, one seeks Nibbāna—the undefiled, unsurpassed security from bondage.
This, monks, is the noble quest.
And I too, monks, before my enlightenment, while still an unenlightened Bodhisatta, by myself...
Being subject to birth, I seek only that which is subject to birth; being myself subject to aging, I seek only that which is subject to aging;
being myself subject to illness, I seek only that which is subject to illness;
being myself subject to death, I seek only that which is subject to death; being myself subject to sorrow, I seek only that which is subject to sorrow.
Being myself subject to defilement, I sought after what was likewise subject to defilement.
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
"Why, being myself subject to birth, do I seek after what is subject to birth? Being myself subject to aging..."
Being subject to birth... being subject to aging... being subject to illness... being subject to death... being subject to sorrow...
being myself subject to defilement, am I seeking only that which is subject to defilement?
What if, being myself subject to birth, having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, I were to seek the unborn, the unsurpassed?
Being myself subject to aging, having understood the danger in that which is subject to aging, I would seek the unaging, unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna;

being myself subject to illness, having understood the danger in that which is subject to illness, I would seek the illness-free, unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna; being myself subject to death...
Being subject to death myself, having understood the danger in being subject to death, may I seek Nibbāna—the deathless, the unsurpassed security from bondage;
being subject to sorrow myself, having understood the danger in being subject to sorrow, may I seek Nibbāna—the sorrowless, the unsurpassed security from bondage;
being subject to defilement myself, having understood the danger in being subject to defilement...
‘May I seek the uncorrupted, unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna. Then, monks,
at a later time, while still young, with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth and in the prime of life,
against the wishes of my weeping parents with tearful faces, I shaved off my hair and beard.
Having shaved off my hair and beard and donned saffron robes, I went forth from the home life into homelessness.
Having thus gone forth, seeking what is wholesome and searching for the supreme state of peace, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma. Having approached him, I said to Āḷāra Kālāma:
“Friend Kālāma, I wish to lead the holy life under this Dhamma and Discipline.”
When this was said, monks, Āḷāra Kālāma said this to me:
“May the venerable one dwell here;
such is this Dhamma that a wise person, in no long time, might by his own direct knowledge realize for himself and abide in the attainment of his own teacher’s doctrine.”
"So, monks, before long, I quickly mastered that Dhamma.
Yet, monks, with only that much—merely by lip-service and mere talk—I claimed the status of one who possesses knowledge and the status of an elder; I and others alike asserted, 'I know, I see.
Then, monks, this occurred to me:"
‘Āḷāra Kālāma does not proclaim this Dhamma merely on the basis of faith alone, saying, “I abide having realized it for myself through direct knowledge and attained it”;
surely Āḷāra Kālāma abides knowing and seeing this Dhamma.
Then, monks, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma; having approached, I said this to Āḷāra Kālāma:
"In what way, friend Kālāma, do you declare that you have, by realizing it for yourself with direct knowledge, attained and dwell in this Dhamma?
When this was said, monks, Āḷāra Kālāma declared the base of nothingness.
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
‘It is not only Āḷāra Kālāma who has faith, I too have faith;
it is not only Āḷāra Kālāma who has energy, I too have energy;
it is not only Āḷāra Kālāma who has mindfulness, I too have mindfulness.’
‘It is not only Āḷāra Kālāma who possesses concentration; I too possess concentration.
It is not only Āḷāra Kālāma who possesses wisdom; I too possess wisdom.
Suppose I were to strive for the realization of that Dhamma which Āḷāra Kālāma declares he dwells in, having realized it for himself through direct knowledge.’”
Then, monks, before long, I quickly realized that Dhamma for myself through direct knowledge, and having attained it, I dwelt therein.
Then, monks, I went to where Āḷāra Kālāma was, and having approached him, I said this to Āḷāra Kālāma:
“Friend Kālāma, have you realized this Dhamma for yourself through direct knowledge, and having attained it, do you proclaim it?”
‘It is to this extent, friend, that I have realized this Dhamma through my own direct knowledge, having attained it, and I proclaim it.
‘It is to this extent, friend, that I too dwell having realized this Dhamma through my own direct knowledge, having attained it.
‘It is a gain for us, friend; it is a great fortune for us, friend!’
We see you, venerable sir, as such a fellow-celibate.

Thus, that Dhamma which I have realized for myself through direct knowledge, having attained it, and proclaim—I abide having realized that very Dhamma for myself through direct knowledge and having attained it;

and that Dhamma which you abide having realized for yourself through direct knowledge and having attained—it is that very Dhamma which I have realized for myself through direct knowledge, having attained it, and proclaim.
"Thus, the Dhamma that I know, you know that same Dhamma; the Dhamma that you know, I know that same Dhamma.
Thus, as I am, so are you; as you are, so am I.
Come now, friend, let us both together lead this community."
"Thus, monks, Āḷāra Kālāma, though he was my teacher, placed me—his own pupil—on an equal footing with himself and honored me with great honor.
Then, monks, it occurred to me:

'This Dhamma does not lead to disenchantment, nor to dispassion, nor to cessation, nor to peace, nor to direct knowledge, nor to enlightenment, nor to Nibbāna; it leads only as far as rebirth in the sphere of nothingness.'"
“Bhikkhus, not finding satisfaction in that Dhamma, I became disillusioned with it and left.
Then, bhikkhus, seeking what is wholesome and searching for the supreme state of sublime peace, I approached Uddaka Rāmaputta and said to him:
‘Friend, I wish to lead the holy life in this Dhamma and Vinaya.’”
When this was said, monks, Udaka Rāmaputta said this to me:
“May the venerable one dwell here;
such is this Dhamma that a wise person, in no long time, might through his own direct knowledge realize for himself and abide in the attainment of his own teacher’s doctrine.”
Thus, monks, before long, I quickly mastered that Dhamma.

But, monks, with only that much—merely by striking my lips and merely by prattling and chattering—I spoke the talk of knowledge and the talk of the elders, and I claimed, both for myself and for others, ‘I know, I see.
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
‘Rāma did not proclaim this Dhamma merely on the basis of faith alone, saying: “Having realized it for myself through direct knowledge, I enter and dwell in it”;
surely Rāma dwelt knowing and seeing this Dhamma.
Then, monks, I approached Udaka Rāmaputta; having approached, I said this to Udaka Rāmaputta:
‘To what extent, friend, did Rāma declare: “Having realized this Dhamma for myself through direct knowledge, I abide in its attainment”?
When this was said, monks, Udaka Rāmaputta declared the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Then, monks, it occurred to me:
‘It was not only Rāma who had faith; I too had faith.
It was not only Rāma who had energy; I too had energy.
It was not only Rāma who had mindfulness; I too had mindfulness.’
‘It was not only Rāma who possessed concentration; I too possess concentration.
It was not only Rāma who possessed wisdom; I too possess wisdom.
Suppose I were to strive for the realization of that Dhamma which Rāma declared he had entered upon and dwelt in, having realized it for himself through direct knowledge.’”
Then, monks, before long, I quickly realized that Dhamma through my own direct knowledge, attained it, and dwelt in it.
Then, monks, I went to where Udaka Rāmaputta was, and having approached him, I said this to Udaka Rāmaputta:
“Friend, did Rāma declare that he had realized this Dhamma through his own direct knowledge, attained it, and dwelt in it to this extent?”
‘To this extent, friend, Rāma declared this Dhamma after having realized it for himself through direct knowledge, having attained it and entered upon it.
‘I too, friend, to this extent dwell having realized this Dhamma for myself through direct knowledge, having attained it and entered upon it.
‘It is a gain for us, friend; it is a great gain for us, friend!’
"We see that you, venerable sir, are such a fellow-celibate as we are.

Thus, that Dhamma which Rāma, having realized it for himself through direct knowledge, attained and entered upon, and then proclaimed—that very Dhamma you dwell having realized for yourself through direct knowledge and attained.

That Dhamma which you dwell having realized for yourself through direct knowledge and attained—that very Dhamma Rāma, having realized it for himself through direct knowledge, attained and proclaimed."
"Thus, that Dhamma which Rāma directly knew, you know that Dhamma; that Dhamma which you know, Rāma directly knew.
Thus, as Rāma was, so are you; as you are, so was Rāma.
Come now, friend, lead this community."
"Thus, bhikkhus, Udaka Rāmaputta, though he was my fellow celibate practitioner, placed me in the position of a teacher and honored me with great honor.
Then, bhikkhus, it occurred to me:

'This Dhamma does not lead to disenchantment, nor to dispassion, nor to cessation, nor to peace, nor to direct knowledge, nor to enlightenment, nor to Nibbāna; it leads only as far as rebirth in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.'"
Thus, monks, not finding satisfaction in that Dhamma, I became disillusioned with it and departed.
Seeking what was wholesome and searching for the supreme state of peace, I wandered by stages through Magadha until I arrived at Uruvelā, the village of Senāni.
There I saw a delightful stretch of land, a charming grove of trees, and a river flowing with clear, white water and pleasant landing-stairs, lovely and with a village nearby for alms.
Then, monks, this occurred to me:

"How delightful indeed is this stretch of land! How beautiful is this grove of trees! And how lovely is this river that flows with white sands and fine landing places! And there is a village for alms nearby.
This is truly sufficient for a clansman seeking to strive in his exertion."
Then, monks, I sat right there, thinking:
"This is sufficient for striving.
And so, monks, being myself subject to birth, having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, [I set my mind] on the unborn.
While seeking the unsurpassed security from bondage that is Nibbāna, I attained the unborn, unsurpassed security from bondage that is Nibbāna;
being myself subject to aging, having understood the danger in what is subject to aging,
and while seeking the ageless, unsurpassed security from bondage that is Nibbāna, I attained the ageless, unsurpassed security from bondage that is Nibbāna.
Being myself subject to illness, having understood the danger in what is subject to illness, while seeking the illness-free,
unsurpassed security from bondage that is Nibbāna, I attained the illness-free,

unsurpassed security from bondage that is Nibbāna; being myself subject to death, having understood the danger in what is subject to death, [I sought] the deathless, unsurpassed security from bondage that is Nibbāna...
Having myself been subject to the nature of sorrow, and having understood the danger in that which is subject to sorrow,
I attained the sorrowless, unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna; having myself been subject to the nature of defilement, and having understood the danger in that which is subject to defilement,
while seeking the undefiled, unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna, [I attained] the undefiled, unsurpassed...
I attained Nibbāna, the security from bondage.
And knowledge and vision arose in me:
"Unshakable is my liberation; this is my last birth; now there is no further becoming."
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
"This Dhamma that I have attained is profound, hard to see, difficult to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise.
Yet this generation delights in attachment, takes delight in attachment, and rejoices in attachment."

"Indeed, for people who delight in attachment, who rejoice in attachment, and who revel in attachment, this matter is difficult to see—that is to say, specific conditionality and dependent origination.
This matter too is difficult to see—that is to say, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
If I were to teach the Dhamma and others did not understand me, that would be weariness to me, that would be vexation to me."
And furthermore, monks, these marvelous verses, never heard before, occurred to me:
“It has been attained by me with difficulty;
enough now with proclaiming it!
This Dhamma is not easily awakened to by those overcome by lust and hatred;
it goes against the stream and is subtle.
‘Profound, hard to see, and subtle;
those stained by passion do not perceive it,
being shrouded by a mass of darkness.’”
"Thus, monks, as I reflected, my mind inclined toward inaction rather than to teaching the Dhamma.
Then, monks, the Brahma Sahampati, knowing with his own mind the reflection in my mind, thought:

'Alas, the world is perishing! Alas, the world is being destroyed! For the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, inclines his mind toward inaction rather than to teaching the Dhamma.'"
Then, monks, Brahmā Sahampati— just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm— disappeared from the Brahma-world and appeared before me. Then, monks,
Brahmā Sahampati arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward me in reverential salutation, and said this to me:
“Teach the Dhamma, Bhante; let the Sugata teach the Dhamma.
There are beings with little dust in their eyes who are perishing through not hearing the Dhamma.
There will be those who understand the Dhamma.”
This, monks, Brahmā Sahampati said.
Having said this, he further spoke as follows:
"In the past, [the Dhamma] appeared among the Magadhans."
The Dhamma is impure, conceived by those still stained with defilements;
open this door to the Deathless,
so that they may hear the Dhamma awakened to by the Stainless One.
Just as one standing on the summit of a mountain might see the people all around, even so,
O wise one, does one who consists of the Dhamma [see] in like manner.
Having ascended the palace, O All-Seeing One,
free from sorrow, look down upon the people overwhelmed by grief,
who are overcome by birth and old age.
Arise, O Hero, victor in battle!
Caravan-leader free from debt, wander through the world;
may the Blessed One teach the Dhamma.
‘They will come to understand.
Then, monks, having understood Brahmā’s entreaty and out of compassion for beings, I surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye.

Surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, monks, I saw beings with little dust on their eyes and those with much dust on their eyes, Please provide the text you would like me to translate. I am ready to assist you.
There were those with keen faculties and those with dull faculties; those of good disposition and those of bad disposition; those easy to instruct and those difficult to instruct;
some dwelling as perceivers of the fear of blame and the next world, while others dwelt as non-perceivers of the fear of blame and the next world.
It was just as if, in a bed of blue lotuses, or red lotuses, or white lotuses, some of the lotuses...
Or there are water-born blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses, grown in the water, developed in the water, not rising above the water, nourished while submerged within it;

and some of those blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses, born in the water, developed in the water, not rising above the water, remain level with the surface of the water; and some of those blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses...
or born in water, grown up in water, yet standing out above the water and unsullied by it;
even so, monks, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, I saw beings with little dust on their eyes and with much dust on their eyes,
with keen faculties and with dull faculties, of good disposition and of bad disposition, easy to instruct and difficult to instruct.
Some were dwelling seeing fear in the other world and in wrongdoing, while others were dwelling not seeing fear in the other world and in wrongdoing.
Then, monks, I replied to Brahmā Sahampati with a verse:
“The doors to the Deathless have been opened for them.”
"Let those who have ears release their faith!
Perceiving harm, O Brahmā,
I did not speak this sublime Dhamma among men."

Then, monks, Brahmā Sahampati, thinking, “I have been granted permission by the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma,” paid homage to me, circumambulated me keeping me to his right, and vanished right there.
Then, monks, this thought occurred to me:
“To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?”
‘Who will understand this Dhamma quickly?
Then, monks, it occurred to me:
‘This Āḷāra Kālāma is wise, competent, and intelligent; for a long time he has been one whose nature is free from much defilement.’”
"What if I were to teach this Dhamma first to Āḷāra Kālāma?
He will quickly understand this Dhamma.
Then, monks, deities approached me and said this:
‘Venerable sir, Āḷāra Kālāma died seven days ago.
And the knowledge and vision arose in me:
‘Āḷāra Kālāma died seven days ago.’
Then, monks, it occurred to me:
"Āḷāra Kālāma is a great man of few wants.
If he were to hear this Dhamma, he would quickly understand it."
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
"To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?
Who will understand this Dhamma most quickly?"
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
“This Udaka Rāmaputta is wise, competent, and intelligent; for a long time he has been one whose vision is largely free from dust.
Suppose I were to teach the Dhamma first to Udaka Rāmaputta.”
‘He will understand this Dhamma very quickly.
Then, monks, deities approached me and said this:
‘Venerable sir, Udaka Rāmaputta has passed away during the last watch of the night.’”
"And knowledge and vision arose in me:
‘Uddaka Rāmaputta has been dead for a week.
Then, monks, this occurred to me:"
“Uddaka Rāmaputta is indeed a great man of noble lineage.
If he were to hear this Dhamma, he would quickly understand it.
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
‘To whom, indeed, should I first teach the Dhamma?
Who will understand this Dhamma quickly?
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
‘The group-of-five monks have been very helpful to me; they attended upon me when I was intent on striving.
What if I were to teach the Dhamma first to the group-of-five monks?
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
‘Where now are the bhikkhus of the group-of-five dwelling?
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I saw, monks, the bhikkhus of the group-of-five dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
Then, monks, having dwelt at Uruvelā for as long as I pleased, I set out on a wandering tour toward Bārāṇasī.
“Bhikkhus, while I was traveling on the road between Gayā and the Bodhi tree, the Ājīvaka Upaka saw me.
Having seen me, he said this to me:
‘Friend, your faculties are serene; your complexion is pure and bright.’”
“Under whom have you gone forth, friend? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you profess?
When this was said, monks, I addressed the Ājīvaka Upaka with these verses:
“I am the conqueror of all, the knower of all;”
Unstained by any phenomena,
having abandoned everything and being liberated through the destruction of craving—
having realized this for myself, whom should I point to as my teacher?
I have no teacher,
and my equal is not to be found;
in this world with its devas, [there is none].
There is no one who is my equal.
For I am the Worthy One in the world;
I am the unsurpassed Teacher.
I am the one and only Fully Enlightened One;
I have become cool and attained Nibbāna.
To set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion—
“I go to the city of Kāsi;
in this world that has become blind,
I shall beat the drum of the Deathless.”
“Friend, as you claim, you are indeed an Arahant,
an infinite Conqueror. “Only those like me are true Conquerors who have attained the destruction of the taints.”
“Evil states have been conquered by me;
therefore, Upaka, I am a Conqueror.
When this was said, monks, the Ājīvaka Upaka replied, “May it be so, friend,” and shaking his head, he took a wrong path and departed.
Then, monks, traveling by stages on my alms-tour, I approached Bārāṇasī, the Deer Park at Isipatana, where the group of five monks were staying.
The group of five monks saw me coming from afar;
having seen me, they made an agreement among themselves:
“Friends, this ascetic Gotama is coming—he is one who indulges in abundance, has fallen away from his striving, and has turned back to abundance.
He should neither be saluted nor rise for him; his bowl and robe should not be received.
However, a seat should be set out; if he so desires, he will sit down.”
In whatever way, monks, I approached, in that same way the group-of-five monks were unable to maintain their prior agreement.
Some came out to meet me and received my bowl and robe; some prepared a seat; some set out water for washing the feet.
Nevertheless, they addressed me by name and with the familiar term "friend."
When this was said, monks, I spoke thus to the group of five monks:
“Do not address the Tathāgata by name and with the word ‘friend,’ monks.
The Tathāgata is an Arahant, monks, a perfectly enlightened one.”
"Listen, bhikkhus, to the ear; I have attained the Deathless, I instruct you, I teach the Dhamma.

Practicing in accordance with my instruction, before long you yourselves will, in this very life, realize for yourselves the supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness."
‘...having realized them through direct knowledge, you shall enter and dwell in them.
When this was said, monks, the group-of-five monks said this to me:
‘Friend Gotama, even by that conduct, by that practice, and by that performance of austerities, you did not attain [superhuman states].’”
“Superhuman states, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones— how could you, who are now luxurious,
have abandoned your striving, and have turned back to luxury, ever attain such superhuman states, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones?
When this was said, monks, I said this to the group of five monks:
“Monks, the Tathāgata is not one who indulges in abundance, nor is he one who has strayed from his striving, nor has he turned back toward abundance.
Monks, the Tathāgata is an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Give ear, monks; the Deathless has been attained. I shall instruct you; I shall teach the Dhamma.”
"Practicing in accordance with what has been instructed, before long you will,

by realizing it for yourselves through direct knowledge, enter and abide in that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness."
A second time, monks, the group-of-five bhikkhus said this to me:

“Friend Gotama, by that conduct, by that practice, and by that performance of austerities, you did not attain any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones; how much less so now, when you have become one who indulges in abundance?”
‘Having fallen away from exertion and turned back toward abundance, will you attain any superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones?
A second time, monks, I said this to the group of five monks:
‘Monks, the Tathāgata does not live in abundance... [and so on].
‘Having attained it, you shall dwell therein.
And for a third time, monks, the group of five monks said this to me:
‘Friend Gotama, even by that conduct, by that practice, and by that performance of austerities, you did not attain [superhuman states].’”
“Superhuman states, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones— how could you, who are now luxurious,
fallen away from exertion, and reverted to luxury, ever attain superhuman states, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones?
When this was said, monks, I said this to the group of five monks:
“Do you remember, monks, that such a thing was ever proclaimed by me before this?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“Monks, the Tathāgata is an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha.”
"Listen, bhikkhus, to the ear that has reached the Deathless; I instruct you, I teach the Dhamma.

Practicing in accordance with my instruction, before long you yourselves will, in this very life, realize for yourselves the supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness."
‘...having realized them through direct knowledge, you shall enter and dwell therein.
And so, monks, I was able to convince the group of five monks.
Indeed, monks, I would instruct two monks while three monks went out for alms.
Whatever three bhikkhus brought back after wandering for alms, by that we, the group of six, sustained ourselves.
Indeed, bhikkhus, I would instruct those three bhikkhus while two bhikkhus wandered for alms;
whatever those two bhikkhus brought back after wandering for alms, by that we, the group of six, sustained ourselves.
Then, monks, while being thus exhorted and instructed by me, the group-of-five monks— being themselves subject to birth,
having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, and seeking the unborn,
supreme security from bondage that is Nibbāna— attained the unborn, supreme security from bondage that is Nibbāna. Being themselves...

Being subject to aging, having understood the danger in that which is subject to aging, and seeking the ageless, supreme security from bondage that is Nibbāna, they attained the ageless, supreme security from bondage that is Nibbāna; being themselves subject to illness...
[and so on] ...being themselves subject to death... being themselves subject to sorrow... being themselves subject to defilement.
Having understood the danger in phenomena subject to defilement, and while seeking the undefiled, unsurpassed security from bondage that is Nibbāna,
they attained the undefiled, unsurpassed security from bondage that is Nibbāna.
And knowledge and vision arose within them:
‘Our liberation is unshakable; this is the last birth; now there is no further existence.
Monks, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure.
What are the five?
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust;
sounds cognizable by the ear … smells cognizable by the nose … [and so forth].
Tastes cognizable by the tongue...
tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust.
These, monks, are the five strands of sensual pleasure.

“Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins, being tied to these five cords of sensual pleasure, infatuated with them, and utterly absorbed in them, enjoy them without seeing the danger and lacking the wisdom of escape—they should be understood as follows:
‘They have met with calamity, they have met with disaster; they are at the disposal of the Evil One to do with as he pleases.
It is just as if, bhikkhus, a forest deer, having been caught, were to lie down upon a heap of snares.”
Thus he should understand this:
"I have fallen into misfortune, I have met with calamity, and I am at the hunter's disposal to do with as he wishes;
moreover, when the hunter arrives, I will not be able to escape wherever I desire."

In the same way, monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins enjoy these five cords of sensual pleasure—being tied to them, infatuated with them, and deeply attached to them, seeing neither the danger nor possessing the wisdom for escape—they should be understood thus:
"They have met with ruin, they have met with disaster; they are at the disposal of the Evil One as he wishes."

"But those ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus, who enjoy these five cords of sensual pleasure without being tied to them, infatuated with them, or blindly absorbed in them, but who see the danger in them and possess the wisdom of escape—they should be understood thus:
'They have not met with misfortune, they have not met with disaster, and the Evil One cannot do with them as he pleases.
Just as a wild forest deer, bhikkhus, that is unbound might lie down upon a heap of snares."
Thus it should be understood of him:
"He has not fallen into misfortune, nor has he met with calamity, nor is he at the hunter's disposal to do as he pleases;
rather, when the hunter arrives, he will depart wherever he wishes."

“In the same way, bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins enjoy these five cords of sensual pleasure without being tied to them, infatuated with them, or blindly absorbed in them, but who see the danger in them and possess the wisdom of escape—they should be understood thus:
‘They have not fallen into ruin, they have not met with disaster, and the Evil One cannot do with them as he pleases.
Just as, bhikkhus, a forest deer wandering in the forest glade goes about confidently, stands confidently, sits down confidently, and lies down confidently.”
For what reason?
Because, monks, he has gone beyond the range of the hunter.

In the same way, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
“Monks, this monk is said to have blinded Māra, left him trackless, and having struck down Māra’s eye, gone beyond the sight of the Evil One.

Furthermore, monks, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a monk enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied thought and without sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
This monk, monks, is said to have blinded Māra … [as before] … gone beyond the sight of the Evil One.”
Furthermore, monks, with the fading away of rapture, a monk dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending;
he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: "He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in happiness.
Thus he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.
This, monks, is called [a monk who has entered the stream] … [leading] to the destruction of the Evil One.
Furthermore, monks, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief,
a monk enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
This, monks, is called [a monk who has escaped] from the Evil One...

Furthermore, monks, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking ‘space is infinite,’ a monk enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
This, monks, is called [a monk who has escaped] from the Evil One...
Furthermore, monks, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking ‘consciousness is infinite,’ a monk enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.
This, monks, is called [a monk who has gone beyond the Evil One]... [as before] ...of the Evil One.
Furthermore, monks, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, thinking ‘there is nothing,’ a monk enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
This, monks, is called [a monk who has transcended the realm of Māra] …pe… of the Evil One.
Furthermore, monks, a monk, by completely transcending the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This, monks, is called [a monk who has transcended the realm of Māra] …pe… of the Evil One.

Furthermore, monks, by completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, a monk enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling; and having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.
This, monks, is called a monk who has blinded Māra, rendered him trackless; having struck down Māra’s eye, he has gone beyond the sight of the Evil One.
Having crossed over the world’s attachment, he moves with confidence, stands with confidence, sits with confidence, and lies down with confidence.
"And for what reason?
Because, monks, he has come outside the range of the Evil One.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The Pāsarāsi Sutta, the sixth, is finished.
